summary: The note traces the history of gyutan (grilled beef tongue) from its invention in postwar Sendai, Japan, by chef Keishiro Sano on September 9th 1948 to its status as a regional, national and global delicacy. It covers Sano's marinating and grilling method, the dish's spread from the late 1950s, modern reinventions, festivals, culinary education, and its role in Sendai's identity.
one_line: Gyutan, grilled beef tongue, was invented in Sendai by Keishiro Sano in 1948 and grew from a local specialty into a global dish.
key_facts: Gyutan (grilled beef tongue) originated shortly after World War II in Sendai, Japan.
Chef Keishiro Sano created gyutan on September 9th 1948, at a time when he owned a yakitori restaurant.
American occupation of Japan after WWII brought beef preferences, and beef tongue had previously been considered foreign fare.
Keishiro Sano noticed that many local residents neglected beef tongue, so he acquired the cut and developed a method to make it tender.
Sano marinated the tongue with special blends of ingredients for hours, grilled it on an indoor gridiron, and served it with barley rice and tail soup.
By the late 1950s, gyutan had become part of Sendai culture and cuisine and later spread beyond Miyagi Prefecture nationwide.
The economic boom of the 1980s brought Japanese cuisine international attention, and gyutan began making waves as part of Japan's food heritage.
After the turn of the millennium, gyutan appeared on international menus, and tourists began visiting Sendai specifically to try it.
In October 2023, Masaru Kamikura introduced a deconstructed version of gyutan at his Tokyo restaurant, combining modern techniques and international flavor.
The Sendai Gyutan Festival celebrated its 65th anniversary on August 5, 2024, attracting thousands of visitors.
The festival featured varied ways to enjoy gyutan, from gyutan sashimi to curry.
Cooking schools in Sendai, including Miyagi Culinary Arts Academy, include gyutan in their curriculums to pass down traditional preparation methods.
Sendai restaurants specializing in gyutan each boast their own secret marinade or cooking method handed down through generations.
